chapter 02 · LLM

What training added

Pretraining produces something that can continue any text and obeys nobody. Everything that makes it an assistant — following your instruction rather than extending it, emitting a tool call, admitting it does not know, stopping — was added afterwards, deliberately, in stages. The single most useful distinction in the field: pretraining creates capability; post-training creates behaviour.

Why a chapter on training in a course about building agents: when your agent misbehaves you must decide whether you are looking at a capability gap or a behaviour gap, because the fixes are different and non-interchangeable. And one fact here is load-bearing for everything after it — tool use is a trained behaviour, not an architectural feature.

01

The stages, and what each one buys

A conceptual decomposition — not a pipeline every lab runs in order.

Read this as a menu of mechanisms rather than a fixed sequence. The published recipes differ, and one of the most cited skips a stage entirely.

StageSignal it learns fromWhat it adds
Pretrainingthe next token, over a corpusCapability. Language, world knowledge, code, latent procedures. Almost everything the model knows.
Mid-trainingmore next-token, domain-weightedShifts the mixture toward a domain without starting over.
SFTdemonstrations written by humansAn interface. Instruction format, role hierarchy, tool-call syntax, worked trajectories. This is where "answer the question" beats "continue the text".
Preference optimization
RLHF · DPO · variants		pairwise judgements: A better than BA policy among plausible answers. Helpful over evasive, qualified over confidently wrong, refusing over complying.
RLVRa checker: tests, a compiler, an answer keyLong chains that end correctly. Rewards the outcome, so it can optimize reasoning no one demonstrated token by token.
Distillationa stronger model's outputsMoves behaviour into a smaller, cheaper model.

The ordering is a convention, not a law. DeepSeek-R1 published a recipe of cold-start SFT → RL → rejection-sampled SFT → more RL → distillation; its sibling R1-Zero omitted the initial SFT entirely and still produced reflection and self-verification from RL alone. Treat any diagram claiming "the" post-training pipeline with suspicion — including the table above.

So: pretraining is where the knowledge comes from, and every later stage is shaping what the model does with it. The next two sections take the two stages that matter most for agents.

02

Preference optimization, read as a loss function

RLHF, DPO, GRPO — three answers to one optimization problem.

The reinforcement-learning framing makes this sound more exotic than it is. The objective is ordinary: maximize a preference score while staying close to the model you started from.

maximize   E[ r(x, y) ]  −  β · KL( π ‖ π_ref )
           └─ preference ─┘     └─ don't drift from the base model ─┘

The KL term is doing real work: without it the policy collapses onto whatever degenerate output scores highest. Everything below is a different way of solving that same objective.

What it doesNeeds
RLHF
classic		Fit a reward model to human pairwise comparisons, then optimize the policy against it under the KL constraint — historically with PPO.a reward model + online rollouts
DPOObserves that the optimal policy for that objective has a closed form, and reparameterizes it into a direct classification loss on preference pairs. The reward model disappears — the policy is its own.just the pairs
GRPOAn online RL optimizer, not a feedback method: drops the learned value baseline and scores each sample relative to others drawn for the same prompt.online rollouts, no critic

DPO is a loss function, and you have read harder ones. That is the whole insight — "your language model is secretly a reward model". If you have ever eliminated a nuisance parameter analytically instead of estimating it, you have done this move. Nothing about DPO requires an RL mental model to understand, and reading it as RL makes it harder than it is.

There is no public "production winner" among the three, and anyone who tells you otherwise is overreading. DPO's paper shows it is simpler and competitive in controlled comparisons; DeepSeek documents GRPO in production; frontier labs disclose too little to infer an industry standard. Choose on what you can supply — pairs, or rollouts — not on which is fashionable.

03

RLVR, and the argument about what it adds

A verifier replaces a human judge — and the field disagrees about what that buys.

Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards swaps the subjective reward model for something mechanical: unit tests, a compiler, an answer checker, a simulator. If the outcome can be checked, the long chain that produced it can be optimized — even though nobody demonstrated that chain.

That matters for agents directly: it is the shape of training that can reward "the thirty-step run ended with a correct artefact" without anyone writing out the thirty steps.

The contested question — and it is genuinely open. Does RLVR add capability the base model did not have, or does it sharpen capability that was already there at low probability?

  • Sharpening: post-training compute is tiny next to pretraining, and the earliest RLHF accounts framed it as unlocking what pretraining already produced. On this view RL raises the probability of traces the base model could already generate, rarely.
  • Something more: R1-Zero reached reflection and self-verification through RL with no SFT at all, which is at least evidence that the behaviour need not be demonstrated to appear.

Both readings survive the published evidence, because probability sharpening alone can produce dramatic multi-step gains — if each step's success rate rises, the compounded effect over a long chain is large without a single new primitive. Do not let anyone collapse this into a settled story in either direction.

Why you should care rather than treat it as lab trivia: it predicts where agent reliability comes from. If sharpening is the mechanism, then a domain with a good verifier gets reliable agents and a domain without one does not — which is exactly the pattern chapter 07 runs into.

04

Tool use is trained, not architectural

The fact chapter 03 rests on.

Nothing in the transformer makes a model good at calling functions. The ability to emit a well-formed call, with correct arguments, at a sensible moment, is a behaviour that was trained in — and it degrades like any other trained behaviour.

evidence

Toolformer — a model trained to decide whether, when and how to call an API, and to fold the result back into its own text.

Tool use was the thing being taught, not a side effect of scale.

evidence

Gorilla — found frontier base models prone to wrong arguments and outright hallucinated APIs; fine-tuning plus retrieval fixed it.

Left untrained, the failure mode is not refusal — it is a confident call to a function that does not exist.

consequence

Chat alignment does not transfer to agents.

Anthropic reported that Claude 4's predominantly chat-based RLHF data contained little agentic tool use — and did not adequately suppress harmful behaviour when evaluated as an agent. The training distribution has to match the deployment shape.

Which means part of "tool skill" is not in the weights at all. A schema cannot express a usage convention — when to prefer this tool, what counts as a reasonable argument, what to do when it returns nothing. That is why vendor guidance recommends putting examples in tool definitions, and why a tool's description is prompt rather than documentation (ch 03, §2). You cannot cleanly attribute tool reliability to the model; you are always measuring model and interface together.

05

Using this to diagnose

The payoff: given a misbehaviour, name the stage and know whether prompting can fix it.
What you observeWhere it comes fromCan prompting fix it?
Doesn't know a fact, or knows a stale onepretraining — the corpus and its cutoffNo. Put it in the context instead → ch 05
Can't do the reasoning at all, at any promptpretraining capabilityNo. Different model, or decompose the task
Ignores part of a multi-part instructionSFT / preferenceOften. Restructure the ask; make the constraint checkable
Calls the wrong tool, or invents argumentsSFT + your schema and descriptionUsually — and the fix is normally yours, not the model's
Confidently fabricatespreference training; not a truth guaranteePartly. Real fix is grounding — give it a tool that can check
Drifts or loses the thread after many stepsnot one stage — training, context, tool design, budget→ ch 04, and it is mostly your side

The last row is the honest one. "Stays on task for thirty steps" has no single owner: it needs agentic training where that exists, but also context engineering, tool design, termination rules and inference budget. When a long run falls apart, the model is the least likely thing you can change and usually not the thing at fault.

You can now say, for a given misbehaviour, which stage is responsible and whether prompting can repair it — and why tool-calling is a trained behaviour rather than a feature of the architecture.

Next: you have a model that follows instructions and emits tool calls. Everything it knows about the run so far lives in one place, re-read from scratch on every step. Managing that is chapter 04.
